solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Dad writing stuff, more unwell apparently – here’s the solution (10)

indicators.note: ILLER is not a real word, so the setter flags that 'more unwell' is only apparently spelt that way

blocks.note: ink is the stuff you write with
ill + -er, a comparative that only looks like a word

annotation.surface: A parent with a headache, scribbling away and feeling worse, announces that relief has arrived.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' admits that ILLER is not good English (the proper form is 'worse'), but it is what 'more unwell' would be if you built it by rule.
annotation.definitionFit: A painkiller is the solution to pain: 'solution' here is the remedy, with a nod to a solution in a medicine bottle.

entries.clue: The old man‘s two secretaries (4)

blocks.note: a PA, personal assistant, is a secretary

annotation.surface: Someone's father, or boss, keeps two secretaries on the payroll.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The old man' is slang for father as well as for the boss, and the boss is the reading the secretaries push you towards.
annotation.definitionFit: Papa is a word for father, and 'the old man' is informal for one's father.

entries.clue: Base in which international poor belong (7)

indicators.note: the I is put in among the letters to be mixed
the letters of BELONG are in poor shape, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, joined by the I

annotation.surface: A remark about a base, perhaps a society's lowest rung, where the world's poor are said to belong.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like a noun (a place where people belong) but it is the adjective meaning low and dishonourable.
annotation.definitionFit: Base and ignoble both mean mean-spirited, lacking honour.

entries.clue: Learned Ed’s invested in own-label keg brewing (13)

indicators.note: ED's letters are put inside the other letters, as money is put into a business
the letters of OWN-LABEL KEG are stirred up like a brew

blocks.note: the name itself, spelt out; the 's that follows is 'is', not a letter

annotation.surface: A man called Ed has put money into a supermarket's own-brand beer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Learned' reads as a verb (Ed learned something) but is the two-syllable adjective, as in a learned professor.
annotation.definitionFit: Learned (LER-nid) means well read and knowing a great deal, which is knowledgeable.

entries.clue: Pulse advanced – one that’s over fifty (6)

indicators.note: in a down answer, I sits above (over) L

blocks.note: to advance money is to lend it; lent

annotation.surface: A heartbeat reading for an older person, someone past fifty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' plays on the heartbeat a doctor takes from someone over fifty; it is the edible seed.
annotation.definitionFit: A lentil is a pulse, the dried edible seed of a pod plant.

entries.clue: Get going, playing opponents on electronic device (8)

indicators.note: in a down answer, EN is placed on top of KINDLE

blocks.note: in bridge East and North are on opposing sides, so E and N are playing opponents

annotation.surface: Someone urges a gamer to start up an online match against rivals on a gadget.
annotation.walkthrough: The bridge table has four compass seats; North partners South and East partners West, so any mixed pair such as E and N are opponents.
annotation.definitionFit: To enkindle is to set alight, and so to get something going.

entries.clue: Biblical character as put over in most European countries (4)

indicators.note: AS is turned over, end to end
the turned word goes inside EU

blocks.note: EU, the European Union, holds most European countries; its first letter wraps the front
the U of EU closes the wrap

annotation.surface: A figure from the Bible is shown across most of Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: The EU contains most, but not all, European countries, which is why the setter says 'most'.
annotation.definitionFit: Esau, Jacob's brother, sold his birthright in Genesis.

entries.clue: Set machine-gun to muffle if loud (7)

indicators.note: the gun wraps round the other letters, as a silencer muffles a sound

blocks.note: the end of STEN closes round them

annotation.surface: An instruction to fit a silencer to a machine-gun should it prove too noisy.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sten was a British submachine gun of the Second World War. 'Set' looks like an instruction to set up the gun but is the definition, as jelly sets.
annotation.definitionFit: To set is to go firm, as concrete sets; to stiffen.

entries.clue: After-school study centre? (10)

blocks.note: the surface means the hours after lessons each day; the setter means the years after leaving school altogether
not a homework club but an institution of higher learning; the question mark flags the pun

annotation.surface: A homework club where children go when lessons end.
annotation.walkthrough: 'After-school' suggests the hours after the bell each day; read it as the years after leaving school.
annotation.definitionFit: A university is a centre of study that people attend after they have finished school.

entries.clue: Bridge, popular card game (7)

blocks.note: a floating bridge laid on boats or drums, used by armies
the British name for blackjack, or twenty-one

annotation.surface: A list of card games, with bridge and another favourite.
annotation.walkthrough: Next to 'card game', 'Bridge' is surely the card game too; here it is the thing you cross a river on.
annotation.definitionFit: A pontoon is a floating bridge, and pontoon is also a card game where you aim for twenty-one.

entries.clue: This country rejected stand by Italy originating from another country (7)

indicators.note: UK is thrown back, reading KU
'by' in the sense of 'beside', as in a house by the sea, so WAIT stands next to I

blocks.note: for a British setter this country is the UK; turned round, KU
to stand (and wait) is to wait
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

annotation.surface: Britain turns down a stand-by deal with Italy offered by some foreign country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This country' in a British paper means the UK. 'Stand by' looks like a phrasal verb, but only 'stand' is WAIT; 'by' puts I next to it.
annotation.definitionFit: Kuwaiti describes something from Kuwait, which to a British solver is another country.

entries.clue: Distressed in hearing If by Victorian writer offering everyday fare (7-6)

indicators.note: the words are to be heard, not read

blocks.note: Mrs Beeton wrote the Victorian Book of Household Management

annotation.surface: A Victorian cookery writer is upset by hearing Kipling's poem 'If' read aloud.
annotation.walkthrough: Isabella Beeton's cookbook was a staple of British kitchens, hence 'everyday fare'. 'If' looks like Kipling's poem but is simply the word whether.
annotation.definitionFit: Distressed furniture or leather is made to look worn, as if weather-beaten.

entries.clue: Like a Christie sleuth with verbosity and delicacy (7,6)

blocks.note: Agatha Christie's Hercule Poirot is Belgian

annotation.surface: Poirot at his most long-winded, and at his most fastidious.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Delicacy' seems to be another of Poirot's traits, fastidiousness, beside his verbosity; it is a treat to eat.
annotation.definitionFit: A Belgian waffle is a thick sweet waffle, a delicacy in the sense of a fine food.

entries.clue: Surgical procedure time given by hospital pre-empts oxygen depletion in theatre (5,5)

indicators.note: 'given by' in the sense of 'set beside', so ERA is supplied next to OP
H comes before the oxygen part

blocks.note: an era is a period of time
H = hospital, as on road signs

annotation.surface: A surgeon's operation runs on at the hospital, and the oxygen in the operating theatre runs low.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Theatre' is the operating theatre of the surface, and 'oxygen depletion' looks like one medical phrase; it splits into O and USE.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by kind: an opera house is one particular sort of theatre, and the surface's operating theatre hides that ordinary sense.

entries.clue: Argues with essentially cryptic clues (6)

indicators.note: the essence, or core, of 'cryptic' is its central letter

blocks.note: P is the middle of the seven letters of cRYPtic
a lead is a clue, as in a detective's leads

annotation.surface: Someone who argues, basically in riddles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clues' feels like the crossword's own clues, but here they are the leads a detective follows.
annotation.definitionFit: To plead is to argue a case, as a barrister pleads in court.

entries.clue: Reserved unopened passes for veterans (3,5)

indicators.note: HOLD loses its opening letter

blocks.note: to reserve is to hold (hold a table); HOLD without its first letter
to pass something is to hand it over

annotation.surface: Complimentary passes, still sealed, are kept aside for ex-servicemen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reserved' looks like an adjective describing the passes, but it is the verb HOLD, and 'passes' is a verb too.
annotation.definitionFit: Old hands are experienced people, veterans at something.

entries.clue: Sorry it’s misshapen, it entangled in the middle (8)

indicators.note: the answer sits in the middle of the run of words

annotation.surface: An apology for something that came out bent and tangled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Misshapen' and 'entangled' look like anagram signals, but the answer is lying in plain sight across the words.
annotation.definitionFit: Penitent means sorry for one's wrongdoing.

entries.clue: One’s often fault-finding with our EV – i.e. we’re packing it in (8)

indicators.note: the words pack the answer inside them

annotation.surface: A critic who picks holes in the family's electric vehicle, saying they are giving up on it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Packing it in' sounds like giving up the car; it means the words pack the answer. EV is an electric vehicle.
annotation.definitionFit: A reviewer, a critic, is someone who often finds fault.

entries.clue: Wild devourer leaves nothing in this? (7)

definitions.text: Wild devourer leaves nothing in this?

indicators.note: the letters run wild, rearranged
the O departs from the letters

annotation.surface: A grazing beast eats every leaf in a green place.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: verdure is green vegetation, which a wild devourer strips bare. 'Leaves' pretends to be foliage.
annotation.definitionFit: Verdure is lush green growth, just what a grazing animal would leave nothing of.

entries.clue: Oddly applied dirty broom to decay (3,3)

indicators.note: the rule is applied to the odd-numbered letters only

blocks.note: the count runs on across the words, so letters 7, 9 and 11: bRoOm To

annotation.surface: A filthy broom is used, unusually, to clean up a decaying floor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To' belongs to the fodder, not the joining words, and supplies the final T.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: dry rot names both a fungus and the crumbling it causes in timber, so it can stand for 'decay'.

entries.clue: Students produce this endless fury, impotent in articulation (3,4)

indicators.note: RAGE loses its end letter
WEAK is to be spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: fury = rage, without its last letter

annotation.surface: A student protest: boundless anger that achieves nothing when voiced.
annotation.walkthrough: Rag week is a week of stunts and charity fundraising run by British university students.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the event is staged each year by a university's student union, with stunts and collections for charity.

entries.clue: Account of this person stuck on motorway somewhere in South America, backed up (6)

indicators.note: in a down answer, ME is stuck on top of M
in a down answer, RIO is read upwards

blocks.note: M = motorway, as in the M1

annotation.surface: A travel story about being stuck in a traffic jam on a South American highway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backed up' paints a tailback, but in a down clue it means read from the bottom up.
annotation.definitionFit: A memoir is a personal account of one's life.

entries.clue: Hotel next to rickety age-old bridge that gets shelled (4-6,3)

indicators.note: H is placed beside the mixed letters
the letters are unsteady, falling into a new order

blocks.note: Hotel is H in the phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: A hotel beside a crumbling ancient bridge comes under artillery fire.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shelled' suggests bombardment in a war zone; the egg's shell is peeled off.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: 'shelled' means having the shell peeled off before eating, not coming under fire.

entries.clue: Ran and fell down, scratching tummy briefly (4)

indicators.note: 'scratching' in the sense of scratching a name from a list, crossing it out, so TUM is struck from TUMBLED

blocks.note: to fall down is to tumble
tummy cut short is TUM, removed from TUMBLED

annotation.surface: A child runs, falls over, and scrapes their stomach.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ran' is the colour in the wash, not running feet, and 'scratching' is crossing out, not scraping skin.
annotation.definitionFit: When dye bleeds it runs: 'the colours ran' means they bled.

entries.clue: King visits universities – twinning the French one comes with strings attached (7)

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside the place visited, so the King goes inside the pair of universities
LE is doubled, a pair of twins

blocks.note: U = university; two of them wrap K

annotation.surface: A monarch tours universities to set up town-twinning with France, a deal with conditions attached.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Strings attached' is the idiom for conditions on a deal, which suits a royal visit; the strings are those of an instrument.
annotation.definitionFit: A ukulele is a small guitar-like instrument, one that literally comes with strings.

entries.clue: Old-fashioned prison said: “Flog more” (7)

indicators.note: CELL is to be spoken aloud, which yields SELL

annotation.surface: A reactionary calls for a return to the old jail and more flogging.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flog' is corporal punishment in the surface; in British slang to flog is to sell.
annotation.definitionFit: To outsell is to sell more, and to flog is informal British for to sell.

entries.clue: Bound to study Kew’s borderless garden (4)

indicators.note: 'bound to' in the sense of tied to, so E is fastened on to the front of DEN
a word's borders are its first and last letters; without them KEW is just E

blocks.note: a den is a private study

annotation.surface: A student is set to study Kew Gardens, which has no flower borders.
annotation.walkthrough: Kew is London's Royal Botanic Gardens, which makes 'borderless' look like gardening; it means trimming off the edge letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the most famous garden of all, the one in Genesis where Adam and Eve lived.

entries.clue: Thousand will enter ground and streak thus? (5-5)

definitions.text: Thousand will enter ground and streak thus?

indicators.note: K goes inside the mixed letters
the letters are ground up and reshaped

annotation.surface: A crowd of a thousand will run on to the pitch and streak: in what state?
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a streaker runs across a sports ground naked. 'Ground' looks like a stadium but is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: To streak is to run naked in public, so a streaker is stark-naked.
